articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-Related General License
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the issuance of an amended Iran-related General License on October 29, 2026.
This amendment updates existing authorizations concerning transactions involving Iran, though specific details of the changes were not immediately released.
The issuance aims to clarify the scope of permissible activities under U.S. sanctions programs targeting Iran.

articles.region: North Korea, Democratic Republic of the Congo
articles.headline: OFAC Designates Individuals and Entities Tied to North Korea and DRC
body: OFAC announced new designations targeting individuals and entities connected to North Korea and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) on October 28, 2026.

The North Korea-related designations include Russian and North Korean nationals linked to LIMITED LIABILITY COMPANY ALIS, CHINYONG INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY COOPERATION COMPANY, and FIRST FINANCIAL AND TECHNICAL DEVELOPMENT CENTER.

Additionally, the Rwandan Ministry of Defence and Zigama Credit and Savings Society, a Kigali-based financial institution, were designated under the DRC-related sanctions, with several individuals listed with digital currency addresses on Ethereum and TRON.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks Settles with OFAC for Russia Sanctions Violations
body: Extreme Networks, Inc., a North Carolina-based artificial intelligence and cloud networking solutions provider, has agreed to pay $1,529,685 to settle nine apparent violations of Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations.

Between September 2018 and March 2022, Extreme exported networking equipment and services to Joint Stock Company Moskovskiy Mashinostroitelniy Zavod Avangard (MMZA), a Russian defense manufacturer majority-owned by a designated Russian state-owned company.

OFAC determined the violations were egregious but voluntarily self-disclosed, emphasizing the importance of sanctions-related diligence during acquisitions and continuous vigilance regarding sanctions risks.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends FAQs on Blocking, Rejecting Transactions, and Reporting
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) amended 11 of its Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) on October 26, 2026, pertaining to blocking and rejecting transactions and filing reports with OFAC.
The revised FAQs, numbered 10, 32-36, 41, 42, 49, 50, and 53, clarify when a payment should be blocked or rejected and outline the procedures for reporting these actions.
This update is part of OFAC's ongoing review of its published guidance to ensure information remains current and does not introduce new sanctions programs or designations.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / Sanctions Law Center

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Iran and Russia General Licenses, Removes Belarus and North Korea Designations
body: OFAC announced new Iran-related designations, alongside the removal of certain Belarus and North Korea designations on October 21, 2026.
The agency also issued new Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses and amended Frequently Asked Questions to provide further guidance.
These actions reflect ongoing adjustments to U.S. sanctions policy in response to evolving geopolitical landscapes.

articles.headline: PAIPA Designations Issued with Associated General Licenses
body: On October 19, 2026, OFAC issued designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA).
These designations are accompanied by the issuance of associated General Licenses, which aim to mitigate unintended consequences of the new sanctions.
The PAIPA targets entities and individuals involved in intellectual property theft that harms U.S. economic interests.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License and FAQ
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and a corresponding Frequently Asked Question on October 16, 2026.
This amendment aims to provide updated guidance and clarity regarding permissible transactions and activities involving Venezuela.
The changes are part of OFAC's ongoing efforts to adapt sanctions programs to current policy objectives.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iran-Related and Cuba Entities, Issues New General Licenses
body: OFAC announced new Iran-related designations and a Cuba designation on October 15, 2026.

In conjunction with these actions, the agency issued new and amended General Licenses and Frequently Asked Questions to provide guidance on the scope of the new restrictions and any authorized activities.
These measures underscore the U.S. government's continued pressure on both Iran and Cuba through targeted sanctions.

articles.headline: Venezuela-Related Designation Removed by OFAC
body: On October 14, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the removal of a Venezuela-related designation.
This action indicates a recalibration of sanctions against individuals or entities previously identified as undermining democratic institutions or engaging in corruption in Venezuela.
The specific reasons for the removal were not immediately detailed but typically follow a review of circumstances or changes in behavior.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations on October 13, 2026.
These designations target individuals and entities involved in international drug trafficking and terrorist financing networks.
The action aims to disrupt the financial infrastructure supporting these illicit activities and protect the U.S. financial system from abuse.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks Fined $1.5 Million by OFAC for Russia Sanctions Breaches
body: Extreme Networks, Inc. has agreed to pay $1,529,685 to settle its potential civil liability for nine apparent violations of the Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations.
The violations involved exporting networking equipment and services to a Russian defense manufacturer majority-owned by a designated entity between September 2018 and March 2022.
OFAC determined the violations were egregious and voluntarily self-disclosed, with a portion of the penalty potentially credited against a parallel Department of Justice resolution.

articles.headline: Bank of America Settles with OFAC for $11.6 Million Over Sanctions Violations
body: Bank of America, N.A. has agreed to an $11,662,930 settlement with OFAC for 475 apparent violations of multiple sanctions programs, including those targeting Russia, Belarus, Iran, Burma, Somalia, narcotics, and global terrorism.

The violations stemmed from processing payments involving blocked banks, failing to prioritize alerts for sanctioned customers, not promptly updating watchlists, and mishandling accounts linked to blocked persons.

OFAC determined the violations were non-egregious but largely not voluntarily self-disclosed, leading to a significant penalty as part of a broader $1.21 billion enforcement action by the U.S. Treasury.

articles.headline: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics Fined $175,015 by OFAC
body: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics has agreed to pay $175,015 to settle apparent violations with the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC).
The details of the violations were not immediately released but typically involve breaches of U.S. sanctions programs.
This settlement underscores OFAC's continued enforcement efforts across various industries to ensure compliance with sanctions regulations.

articles.headline: Individual Settles with OFAC for $1.4 Million Penalty
body: An individual has agreed to pay $1,427,230 to settle apparent violations with the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC).
The specific nature of the individual's violations was not detailed in the public announcement.
This enforcement action highlights OFAC's willingness to pursue penalties against individuals who breach U.S. sanctions laws.

articles.headline: Rice Lake Weighing Systems Fined $60,764 for Iran Sanctions Violations
body: Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc., a Wisconsin-based manufacturer, has agreed to pay $60,764 to settle eight apparent violations of OFAC sanctions on Iran.
The violations occurred when its Italian subsidiary exported weighing equipment to Iran through a distributor in the United Arab Emirates, despite knowing the ultimate destination was Iran.

OFAC determined the violations were non-egregious and voluntarily self-disclosed, but emphasized that foreign subsidiaries owned or controlled by U.S. persons are subject to similar obligations as their U.S. parent.

articles.headline: FTI Consulting Settles with OFAC for $1.05 Million Over Russia Sanctions
body: FTI Consulting, Inc., a Washington D.C.-based global advisory firm, has agreed to pay $1,050,000 to settle apparent violations of OFAC sanctions targeting Russia's financial sector.
Between April 2019 and May 2021, FTI indirectly dealt in prohibited debt of VTB Bank OAO, a Russian state-owned bank on OFAC's Sectoral Sanctions Identification List.
OFAC found that FTI extended debt of more than 14 days maturity to VTB by indirectly issuing invoices that went unpaid or were paid long past the permissible tenor.

articles.headline: Adani Enterprises Fined $275 Million by OFAC for Iran Sanctions Breaches
body: Adani Enterprises Limited (AEL), an India-based multinational, has agreed to pay $275,000,000 to settle apparent violations of OFAC sanctions on Iran.

From November 2023 to June 2025, AEL purchased 32 shipments of Iranian-origin liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) disguised as Omani and Iraqi product, causing U.S. financial institutions to process approximately $192 million in payments.
OFAC deemed the violations egregious, citing AEL's commercial sophistication and the harm to U.S. foreign policy objectives, despite mitigating factors such as cooperation and remedial measures.

articles.headline: TradeStation Securities Pays $1.1 Million for Sanctions Violations
body: TradeStation Securities, Inc., a Florida-headquartered brokerage firm, has agreed to pay $1,110,661 to settle 481 apparent violations of multiple OFAC sanctions programs.
For nearly a year, from June 2021 to June 2022, TradeStation provided investment services to customers located in Iran, Syria, and the Crimea region of Ukraine due to compliance control failures.
OFAC determined the violations were non-egregious and voluntarily self-disclosed, highlighting the importance for financial institutions to test and validate compliance tools.

articles.headline: Individual Fined $3.7 Million by OFAC for Syrian Sanctions Breaches
body: A U.S. citizen residing abroad has agreed to pay $3,777,000 to settle liability for 20 apparent violations of the Syrian Sanctions Regulations.
The violations occurred between 2018 and 2021, though specific details of the individual's activities were not publicly disclosed.
This significant penalty underscores OFAC's enforcement against individuals who engage in prohibited transactions with sanctioned jurisdictions.

articles.headline: IMG Academy Settles with OFAC for $1.7 Million Over Narcotics Sanctions Violations
body: IMG Academy, LLC, a U.S.-based academic and athletic training institution, has agreed to pay $1,720,000 to settle 89 apparent violations of OFAC counternarcotics sanctions.

Between 2019 and 2025, IMG Academy entered into tuition enrollment agreements and processed payments for two individuals designated under the Foreign Narcotics Kingpin Designation Act due to their ties to a sanctioned Mexican drug cartel.

OFAC found that routine due diligence, such as screening contracting parties or payors, would have revealed the individuals' names on the SDN List, emphasizing the need for robust sanctions compliance programs in academic institutions.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
